analysis.one_liner: Caps what drug makers can charge for medicines in federal health programs at prices paid abroad.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to six House committees on introduction, sent to a Health subcommittee in July 2025, and has one cosponsor with no committee vote or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Health and Human Services Secretary to set a yearly reference price for every prescription drug, based on the lowest list price charged in twelve other wealthy countries such as Canada, Germany, and Japan. No drug's list price could exceed that reference price in Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, VA care, federal employee coverage, or Indian Health Service care. It would also require manufacturers to offer every individual, insured or not, the drug at the reference price, with fines of five times the excess revenue for manufacturers that overcharge federal programs; collected penalties would go to NIH drug research.
analysis.who_benefits: Enrollees in Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, VA health care, federal employee plans, and Indian Health Service programs, plus uninsured people and anyone with private insurance, who would gain access to drugs at internationally benchmarked prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People on Medicare, Medicaid, VA, and private plans

how_it_helps.text: The Secretary must set an annual reference price for each drug at the lowest retail list price among twelve reference countries, when pricing data is available for at least three of them, and no drug's list price may exceed that reference price for federal health program enrollees [S2].
Manufacturers must offer drugs at the reference price to all individuals, including the uninsured and people in private or employer plans, effectively extending the price cap nationwide [S2].

Manufacturers that overcharge face a civil penalty each year per drug equal to five times the excess revenue collected from federal health programs, with penalty funds transferred to NIH for drug research and development [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose United States prices are generally the highest in the world and who would see a large share of that revenue capped at lower international levels.

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only list prices, not the rebates and discounts that dominate the actual economics of brand drugs, so its real-world effect on what programs and patients pay could be smaller than the headline suggests [S2].

Setting prices by comparing to other countries can reduce expected revenue on new medicines, and critics argue this could slow some research and development; the bill's own penalty-funded NIH research stream acknowledges that research funding depends on drug revenue [S2].

Where pricing data is unavailable for at least three reference countries, the Secretary would set prices based on subjective value judgments, creating uncertainty for manufacturers and possible administrative disputes [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If enacted, the price cap would lower drug spending for federal programs and tens of millions of patients, including capping what uninsured people pay directly. The main costs fall on brand-name manufacturers' revenue, with a possible knock-on to investment in new medicines; whether that trade-off is worth it depends on how much of current US pricing is excess over other countries' comparable markets.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, referred to six House committees, and sent to the Health subcommittee in July 2025; no committee has voted on it and no floor action has occurred since.

narrative.text: Rep. Debbie Dingell introduced the bill on May 14, 2025 [S1].
On introduction it was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Armed Services, Veterans' Affairs, Oversight and Government Reform, and Natural Resources committees [S1].
On July 2, 2025, it was referred to the Health subcommittee, and there have been no further actions, no committee votes, and no floor votes [S4].
The bill has one cosponsor, a Democrat, in addition to its Democratic sponsor [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With the bill stalled in committee, brand-name drug manufacturers keep current US prices unchanged; no patient group benefits yet.

for.name: Rep. Debbie Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill establishing international reference prices for prescription drugs in federal health programs

for.name: One Democratic cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor

sides.party_line_note: No vote has ever been taken; the sponsor and sole cosponsor are both Democrats, but there is no recorded opposition in the congressional record.

industries.note: Their US list prices, among the highest in the world, would be capped at the lowest prices charged in twelve other countries, both for federal programs and for every individual buyer. This would cut substantially into revenue on their biggest market.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug pricing middlemen
industries.note: A hard list-price cap would compress the spread between list prices and net prices that intermediaries currently manage, shrinking the margin on which rebate negotiations operate. The bill does not address their role directly.

Lower capped drug prices would reduce drug spending for private plans and employers, since plan coverage plus cost-sharing cannot exceed the reference price. The benefit passes through to premiums and patients.

analysis.trajectory: A health bill with one cosponsor sitting in the Health subcommittee six months after introduction, split across six committee jurisdictions, rarely reaches the floor. Unless it attracts substantial additional support or a larger drug-pricing vehicle carries its provisions, it is likely to die at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote.
